intro.text: Every term here is a **label for something you already practiced**. If you can explain the idea in the left-hand column and forget the right-hand word, that is a vocabulary-only error and the cheapest kind there is.
The "First met" column points at the exercise where the idea was introduced, not where the word was.

terms.plain: a name pointing at an object
terms.meaning: the name is a label attached to an object, not a box holding a value

terms.plain: giving a name a new object
terms.meaning: the label moves; nothing about the old object changes
both names reach the same object, so a change through one is visible through the other

terms.plain: the object itself, as opposed to what it looks like
terms.meaning: tested with `is` or `id()`; distinct from `==`, which compares appearance
list, dictionary, set — can be altered while every name stays put
number, string, tuple, `True`/`False`, `None` — can only be replaced
e.g. `.append()`, `xs[0] = 1`, `d[k] = v` — no name moves
the object a function hands back when it has nothing to return
counted from 0; negative counts from the end
`xs[a:b]`, stopping before `b`; always produces a new list

terms.plain: may be used as a dictionary key or set item
terms.meaning: the object can be filed by what it looks like and will not change afterward

terms.plain: a copy of the outer container only
terms.meaning: `xs[:]`, `list(xs)`, `dict(d)`, `copy.copy(x)` — inner objects stay shared

terms.plain: a copy all the way down
terms.meaning: `copy.deepcopy(x)` — nothing shared at any level
membership is decided by indentation alone

terms.plain: the order in which lines run
terms.meaning: top to bottom, except where loops and calls redirect it
runs once per pass
the loop variable is rebound at the start of each

terms.plain: the running name a loop keeps updating
terms.meaning: an ordinary name; it survives after the loop ends

terms.plain: the name that builds up a result
terms.meaning: must be bound *before* the loop
list, tuple, string, range, dict, set, file, generator

terms.plain: a one-pass position marker over an iterable
terms.meaning: what `for` makes for you invisibly; `next()` advances it
a generator or iterator that has produced its last value

terms.plain: a recipe that produces values on demand
terms.meaning: holds no items; one pass only

terms.plain: building a list in one expression
terms.meaning: `[expr for x in it if cond]`; produces a new object

terms.plain: pulling several names out of one item
terms.meaning: `k, v = pair` — the same thing `for k, v in ...` does per pass
`range` and generators; contrast the **eager** list comprehension
`def` builds a function object and binds a name to it
`f()` — the parentheses are the call, and nothing else is
bound in a fresh set of names for each call
the objects the caller's expressions produced

terms.plain: the fresh set of names a call gets
terms.meaning: created on entry, gone on return

terms.plain: an inner name hiding an outer one of the same spelling
terms.meaning: they are different names; assigning to one does not touch the other
an object, not a copy of one

terms.plain: a stand-in default meaning "nothing was given"
terms.meaning: usually `None`, because it cannot be changed

groups.title: Words this collection avoids, and why

notes.text: **"Variable."** Not wrong, but it invites the box-and-contents picture. *Name* and *binding* keep the arrow visible. Use "variable" freely once the picture is secure.

**"Value."** Ambiguous between *the object* and *what the object looks like* — precisely the distinction Exercises 1.11 and 4.13 turn on. Say "object" when you mean the thing and "contents" when you mean its appearance.

**"Pass by reference" / "pass by value."** These describe a choice Python does not make. Arguments are bound to parameter names; a caller sees a change if and only if the body changed an object the caller can also reach (8.6). Any sentence starting "Python passes by..." is about to be less accurate than the sentence it replaced.
**"Copy," unqualified.** Always say which level: *shallow* or *deep*. An unqualified "copy" is where the bugs in Stage 4 live.
